title: Ekin Dogus Cubuk - Combining Experiments, LLMs, and Theory to Discover Quantum Materials

segments.text: [APPLAUSE]
Hello everyone.
My name is Dogus Cubuk.
I'm a co-CEO and cofounder of Periodic Labs.
And we combine simulations, experiments, and LLMs
to try to accelerate physical R&D.
So for the next few minutes, I want
to talk about whether AGI, either today's AI
capability or the future AI capability
could just zero-shot the next big scientific breakthrough.
And I say it has to be zero-shot because the breakthrough,
by definition, can't be in the training set.
So it must be something that's different than what's
been done before.
So it has to be done without previous demonstration
for that breakthrough.
Another way of thinking about this
is, can thinkism ever be enough for advancing physics?
So thinkism is this idea that you lock yourself in a room,
and you have all the textbooks, all the previous experiments,
papers, patents ever been done in the field.
And if you think really hard, whether you're
a human, or AGI, or AI, a bunch of agents,
can you advance physics?
And I will argue, for the next few minutes, the answer is no,
because the universe is too complex for any intelligence,
whether it's humans or machines, to think their way
into the scientific advance.
So what's the alternative?
The alternative is what we've done
for centuries, which is, you iterate with the universe.
You have a hypothesis, you try it.
It usually doesn't work on the first one,
but you learn from your failure, and then you keep trying.
So one very interesting history to the study for this topic
is the history of superconductivity.
If you study history of superconductivity,
you learn a lot about humans, science, scientists,
academic publishing, archive, et cetera.
But today, I'll just focus on a few things.
So the superconductivity, for the first time,
was discovered back in 1911.
And it was not discovered because incredible human
just thought really hard and then said,
OK, if you take mercury and figure out
how to lower the temperature, electrons
will feel an attractive force through phonons.
No.
What happened is, Onnes' lab, this lab
led by Kamerlingh Onnes, for the first time,
created a capability that can lower the temperature
below any temperature recorded before.
And it was around four Kelvin.
They got it down to 1.8, but turns out,
for some metals like mercury, if you can get it to four Kelvin,
it will superconduct.
So it was actually a side project of the main effort,
which was to liquefy helium.
And a few years later, Ernest got a Nobel Prize.
But very important to note, Nobel Prize was not
given to superconductor discovery,
it was given to the fact that he could liquefy helium.
And if you look at the rest of the history,
it's full of examples like this, where the big innovation wasn't
done fully intentionally, and it wasn't
done by thinking really hard, but it
was done by trying a bunch of things
and iterating intelligently with the universe.
So another really good example is, around 1958,
John Bardeen and collaborators figured out the theory of BCS
superconductivity.
So this is conventional superconductivity.
And it's great.
Right now, the humans understand how superconductivity works.
We can use that understanding to discover
lots of other superconductors.
But that's not really what happened.
So if you follow this curve from 1958 to around 2000,
there's been really major advances
into conventional superconductivity.
The biggest one, the SODA in deep learning language
is magnesium diboride, MgB2.
But if you look at how that was discovered,
it was not discovered by humans taking the theory,
thinking really hard, and making the material,
it was more like they were trying tens of thousands
of materials, and that particular one happened
to be a really good BCS superconductor.
And of course, the other really good example is the cuprates.
Around 1986, Alex Mueller and collaborators
were able to find the first high temperature superconductor,
the unconventional one.
But if you look at his Nobel Prize speech,
you realize, he was actually trying
to find a conventional superconductor,
because he didn't even know what an unconventional superconductor
would be.
So this is just for superconductors.
But if you look at other aspects of materials science, chemistry,
solid state physics-- so I'm not talking
about math and theoretical computer science,
I think that's a different regime.
But if you look at complex systems like physics, chemistry,
material science, you realize that most things
were found by either accident or a bunch of trial and error.
So if this is the case, what does this
mean for agents and LLMs?
So I think we're fine.
We just have to figure out how to use agents
in the scientific method that we've been
using for hundreds of years.
So a very simple way of looking at it,
we have some observations.
We come up with an hypothesis.
We try the hypothesis through an experiment.
And then we look at the result. It will probably not
work very well in the first time,
but we understand why it failed and we try again.
So this is the typical scientific method,
but how we can improve this with LLMs, and agents,
and machine learning is we can insert it in a bunch of places.
So one example I can give is the simulation part
in the very middle.
So the simulations are already completely
revolutionized by machine learning.
So today, we use force fields, which are approximate quantum
mechanics of the ground state.
And if there is another AI winter,
I can't imagine ever not using machine learning anymore
for force fields.
Another example is, of course, AlphaFold.
Now, we figured out how to do protein folding
way better than before, thanks to machine learning.
But force fields, AlphaFold, these are all tools.
They don't actually give us the next big drug
or the next big superconductor, but they're very useful tools.
And there are other tools, of course,
such as characterization, which helps
us look at the experimental data and figure out what happened.
It's very technical, but AI can really
automate and scale that up.
And at Berkeley here, there's been some frontier work,
showing how you can use robotic arms to try a bunch of things
in the lab for synthesizing powders.
And characterization is the obvious thing
you can improve with AI.
Another example is literature search,
going through all the papers and figuring out
what other ideas to try.
And of course, DOE, Design of Experiment,
where based on all the experiments you've seen so far,
what should be the next experiment?
So in our company and outside our company,
AI is making a huge impact on all of these parts.
And of course, it's not this clean.
It's actually much more complicated.
It's a spaghetti plot, where everything interacts
with each other, but you can easily
see how the whole scientific method can
accelerate if we put AI in it intentionally and carefully.
So my last slide here, I just want to say, in my opinion
and in our company's opinion, this universe
is too complex for thinking alone to innovate.
So instead of looking at the current LLM progress
and getting discouraged, especially
if you're a science student, you should think the opposite.
It's actually a really exciting time to do science.
And what I would recommend is to fully focus
on understanding the fundamentals.
If you're a physicist, study the theory of superconductivity,
study solid state chemistry.
If you're a biologist, study what's important in biology.
I don't know.
And really understand the scientific fundamentals,
experimentation, because you realize that a lot of progress
happened when people came up with new experimental methods,
new techniques, new measurement tools.
And you can contribute to all of these.
And as you create new experimentation methods,
new tools, then AI will benefit from it,
because AI will see more data, and they'll
be able to use this thinkism skill to make sense
out of it faster, in bigger scale.
And then hopefully, the next experiment you try
is more successful and more intelligent.
Thank you.
[APPLAUSE]
